analysis.answer: Under current law, each county decides for itself whether its jail will honor federal immigration detainer requests. This measure replaces that local choice with a statewide mandate, requiring all county jails to honor these requests and hold individuals for up to 48 extra hours.

Direct costs fall on counties, which must pay to house, feed, and supervise individuals for up to 48 additional hours. There are also opportunity costs for jail bed space, and potential legal costs if counties face litigation over the constitutionality of extended holds.

Federal immigration authorities benefit from the guaranteed window to take individuals into custody without needing to track them down post-release. County governments and local taxpayers bear the financial burden of the extended detention. Immigrants subject to the detainers bear the cost of extended incarceration and subsequent federal custody.

Undocumented immigrants and mixed-status families may avoid interacting with local police or utilizing government services due to fear that any arrest, even for minor offenses, will lead to deportation. Local law enforcement may need to adjust jail operations to accommodate the mandatory holds.

The measure addresses the issue of federal immigration authorities lacking sufficient time to take custody of individuals being released from local jails, as well as the inconsistency of county-by-county policies. The mechanism—a mandatory 48-hour hold—standardizes the rule and guarantees a time window for federal agents to arrive.
The state legislature and federal immigration authorities gain power, while county governments and local sheriffs lose the discretion to manage their jails according to local policy preferences.

The effect of mandatory immigration cooperation on public safety is disputed. Some researchers find that such policies reduce crime by ensuring the removal of individuals who have committed offenses, while others find that they increase crime by chilling community cooperation with law enforcement, making victims and witnesses less likely to report crimes.
